description: The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive space survival game where players manage a Moon or Mars base. They must balance oxygen, food, water, power, and radiation protection while handling emergencies like solar storms and equipment failures. Each choice affects the crew and mission, helping students learn how astronauts solve problems and manage limited resources in space.
summary:
Outpost Zero is a free browser game for kids 7-12, where players run a Moon outpost for 14 sols (days). Each sol they split 8 units of power between life support, grow lights, radiation shielding and science. Every choice costs something: shielding protects the crew but slows research, and skipping life support drains the air. A “ghost preview” shows tomorrow’s result before players commit, so they learn to weigh trade-offs and plan around a storm forecast.

The sky comes from real NASA data. Live mode turns the last 14 days of solar flares from NASA DONKI into daily storm levels. Archived modes replay the 2003 Halloween storms and the May 2024 superstorm. After each sol, a “Why?” card explains what happened and links to NASA OSDR, DONKI and Artemis resources. Real, archived and simulated data are clearly badged, and DATA_SOURCES.md documents every simplification.

It matters because future Moon and Mars crews will make these trade-offs every day. Outpost Zero lets children practice that thinking and see space weather as a real, changing hazard. It needs no install or account.
details:
Outpost Zero is a browser game for kids 7-12 in which players run a Moon outpost for 14 sols (days). Each sol they split 8 units of power between four systems: life support, grow lights, shielding and science. Three meters track the result: air, radiation dose (which never goes down) and science points. Players win by reaching 250 science points without running out of air or reaching a dose of 100.

The sky is the challenge. Each day has a storm level from calm to extreme, shown with a one-day forecast. Live mode reads the last 14 days of solar flares from NASA’s DONKI service and maps flare class (C, M or X) to a storm level. Archived modes replay the Halloween storms of 2003 and the May 2024 superstorm. A random mode is there for practice. A “ghost preview” shows tomorrow’s air, dose and science on the bars before the player commits. After each sol, a “Why?” card explains what happened in plain language and links to NASA OSDR, DONKI or Artemis pages. Random Moon-dust days cut the power budget from 8 to 6.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Kids practice the real tension in mission planning: protecting the crew costs research, and nothing is free.
  • They see that space weather is a daily, changing hazard, not a fixed backdrop.
  • It needs no install, account or sign-up. Opening index.html is enough, and it falls back to archived data if the live feed is unavailable.

The goal is to build early intuition for systems trade-offs and curiosity about NASA research.

Tools and technology

  • HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks or build step.
  • NASA DONKI (flare endpoint) for live data, with archived flare classes in data.js.
  • NASA OSDR and Artemis pages as linked learning resources.
  • It runs in any modern browser on desktop or mobile, so no special hardware is needed.

Creativity

  • The game has no safe option. Every choice moves another meter the wrong way.
  • Real storms drive the gameplay instead of a theme painted over it.
  • The ghost preview makes the trade-off visible before the player commits.
  • Failure is framed as how engineers learn, and each sky plays differently.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty about data: every sky is badged LIVE, ARCHIVED or SIMULATED, and DATA_SOURCES.md lists what is real and what is simplified. The power budget, dust events and meter formulas are game simplifications.
  • Flares as a proxy: flares are a stand-in for the true hazard, solar energetic particles. Reading DONKI’s SEP endpoint is a planned next step.
  • Age fit: short sessions, large buttons, plain-language explanations and a clear definition of dose on the start screen.
  • Reliability: a graceful fallback when the live feed fails or rate-limits the shared demo key.
  • Learning over scoring: each “Why?” card ties the player’s last choice to a real NASA concept.
